Aguinaldo, welcome back to the show. Today, a different topic: the new metro line. Should it go to a private operator?
It is likely to be the best option, but only with a good contract. In plain English, the operator has to buy the rolling stock and run the trains, as long as the state builds the tunnel.
And who pays if nobody uses the line?
That is the real question. Ridership tends to ramp up slowly, over three or four years. So the contract usually says that the state pays the difference in the first years.
Our listeners say the trains on line two are already overcrowded.
They are. Line two carries two million people a day — or rather, one point eight million. The new line should take part of that, and reduce congestion downtown.
And the fare? Will it go up?
Not in the first five years. The fare can only change if the agency approves it. That is in the contract, and it is binding.

Good morning. One year ago we opened Line Six, and I want to give you the numbers honestly. Ridership in the first year was roughly three hundred thousand passengers a day. The forecast was four hundred thousand. So we are below the forecast, and I am not going to pretend that we are not. But I do not see it as a failure. Ridership on a new line usually ramps up over three or four years, as people change their routines and their jobs. We expect it to grow steadily. And there is one more reason to be optimistic. Next year we open the connection with the central transit hub, where four lines and most of the bus routes meet. That connection is likely to bring the biggest increase in ridership of the whole project. Questions?

I have worked on ridership forecasts for twenty-five years, and I can tell you one thing with confidence: they are usually wrong, and they are usually wrong in the same direction. They are too high. Studies of transport projects around the world show that most of them overestimate demand, sometimes by a lot. Why? The most common reason is not bad mathematics. It is optimism about the connections. The forecast assumes that the new line will connect with the other lines and the buses on day one. In real life, those connections arrive late, sometimes years late. So my recommendation for any concession contract is simple. Do not give all the demand risk to one party. Share it between the state and the operator in the first years, until the ridership is real.
